source: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held on her way north-eastward towards the island of Java; a gentle air impelling her keel, so that in the surrounding serenity her three tall tapering masts mildly waved to that languid breeze, as three mild palms on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, alluring jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost preternatural spread over the sea, however unattended with any stagnant calm; when the long burnished sun-glade on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, enjoining some secrecy; when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on; in this profound hush of the visible sphere a strange spectre was seen by Daggoo from the main-mast-head.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, and disentangling itself from the azure, at last gleamed before our prow like a snow-slide, new slid from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, as slowly it subsided, and sank. Then once more arose, and silently gleamed. It seemed not a whale; and yet is this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but on re-appearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his nod, the negro yelled out—“There! there again! there she breaches! right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!”

Upon this, the seamen rushed to the yard-arms, as in swarming-time the bees rush to the boughs. Bare-headed in the sultry sun, Ahab stood on the bowsprit, and with one hand pushed far behind in readiness to wave his orders to the helmsman, cast his eager glance in the direction indicated aloft by the outstretched motionless arm of Daggoo.

Whether the flitting attendance of the one still and solitary jet had gradually worked upon Ahab, so that he was now prepared to connect the ideas of mildness and repose with the first sight of the particular whale he pursued; however this was, or whether his eagerness betrayed him; whichever way it might have been, no sooner did he distinctly perceive the white mass, than with a quick intensity he instantly gave orders for lowering.

The four boats were soon on the water; Ahab’s in advance, and all swiftly pulling towards their prey. Soon it went down, and while, with oars suspended, we were awaiting its reappearance, lo! in the same spot where it sank, once more it slowly rose. Almost forgetting for the moment all thoughts of Moby Dick, we now gazed at the most wondrous phenomenon which the secret seas have hitherto revealed to mankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs in length and breadth, of a glancing cream-colour, lay floating on the water, innumerable long arms radiating from its centre, and curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as if blindly to clutch at any hapless object within reach. No perceptible face or front did it have; no conceivable token of either sensation or instinct; but undulated there on the billows, an unearthly, formless, chance-like apparition of life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, with a wild voice exclaimed—“Almost rather had I seen Moby Dick and fought him, than to have seen thee, thou white ghost!”
“The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships ever beheld, and returned to their ports to tell of it.”
But Ahab said nothing; turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel; the rest as silently following.

Whatever superstitions the sperm whalemen in general have connected with the sight of this object, certain it is, that a glimpse of it being so very unusual, that circumstance has gone far to invest it with portentousness. So rarely is it beheld, that though one and all of them declare it to be the largest animated thing in the ocean, yet very few of them have any but the most vague ideas concerning its true nature and form; notwithstanding, they believe it to furnish to the sperm whale his only food. For though other species of whales find their food above water, and may be seen by man in the act of feeding, the spermaceti whale obtains his whole food in unknown zones below the surface; and only by inference is it that any one can tell of what, precisely, that food consists. At times, when closely pursued, he will disgorge what are supposed to be the detached arms of the squid; some of them thus exhibited exceeding twenty and thirty feet in length. They fancy that the monster to which these arms belonged ordinarily clings by them to the bed of the ocean; and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, is supplied with teeth in order to attack and tear it.

There seems some ground to imagine that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppodan may ultimately resolve itself into Squid. The manner in which the Bishop describes it, as alternately rising and sinking, with some other particulars he narrates, in all this the two correspond. But much abatement is necessary with respect to the incredible bulk he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature, here spoken of, it is included among the class of cuttle-fish, to which, indeed, in certain external respects it would seem to belong, but only as the Anak of the tribe.

modern_en.title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — though with no stagnant calm about it — when the long burnished path of sunlight on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the negro yelled out, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

At this the seamen rushed out to the yardarms, the way bees rush to the branches at swarming time. Ahab stood bareheaded on the bowsprit in the sweltering sun, one hand thrust far behind him, ready to signal his orders to the helmsman, and turned his eager gaze in the direction that Daggoo's outstretched, motionless arm was pointing from aloft.

Perhaps the drifting company of that one still, solitary jet had slowly worked on Ahab, so that he was now ready to link ideas of mildness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he was hunting; or perhaps his eagerness got the better of him. Whichever it was, the moment he clearly made out the white mass, he gave orders, with quick intensity, to lower the boats.

The four boats were soon in the water, Ahab's in the lead, all pulling hard toward their prey. Soon the thing went down, and as we waited, oars raised, for it to reappear — look! — it slowly rose again in the very spot where it had sunk. Almost forgetting Moby Dick for the moment, we now stared at the most astonishing phenomenon the secret seas have yet revealed to mankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs long and wide, of a gleaming cream color, lay floating on the water, with countless long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as though groping blindly for any unlucky object within reach. It had no face or front that could be made out, no conceivable sign of either feeling or instinct; it simply rippled there on the waves, an unearthly, shapeless, chance-like apparition of life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I would almost rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him than have seen you, white ghost!"
"What was it, sir?" said Flask.
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions sperm whalemen in general have attached to the sight of this object, one thing is certain: because a glimpse of it is so very rare, that fact alone has done much to give it an air of ill omen. It is seen so seldom that, although every one of them declares it the largest living thing in the ocean, very few have more than the haziest notions of its real nature and shape. Even so, they believe it provides the sperm whale with his only food. Other kinds of whales find their food above water, where men can watch them eating; but the spermaceti whale gets all his food in unknown zones below the surface, and what exactly it consists of can only be worked out by inference. Sometimes, when hard pressed, he will throw up what are thought to be the detached arms of the squid, some of them more than twenty, even thirty, feet long. The whalemen imagine that the monster these arms belonged to usually clings by them to the ocean floor, and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, has teeth so that he can attack it and tear it apart.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppodan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classed among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward respects it would seem to belong — but only as the Anak of the tribe — its biblical giant.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 59 — Blæksprutten
paragraphs: Pequod vadede langsomt gennem brit-engene og holdt stadig kursen nordøst mod øen Java. En blid brise skubbede på hendes køl, så hendes tre høje, spidst tilløbende master i den omgivende ro svajede mildt i den dovne vind, som tre palmer på en slette. Og stadig, med store mellemrum i den sølvfarvede nat, blev den ensomme, lokkende stråle set.

Men en gennemsigtig blå morgen, da en næsten overnaturlig stilhed bredte sig over havet — dog uden noget stillestående vindstille over sig — da den lange, polerede sti af sollys på vandet lignede en gylden finger, lagt hen over det som befaling om hemmelighed, da de tøffelklædte bølger hviskede sammen, mens de blidt løb videre — i denne dybe hvile i den synlige verden blev et mærkeligt syn set af Daggoo fra stormastetoppen.

I det fjerne steg en stor hvid masse dovent op, og mens den steg højere og højere og løsrev sig fra det blå, glimtede den til sidst foran vores stævn som et sneskred, der lige er gledet af bjergene. Efter at have glitret således et øjeblik sank den langsomt. Så steg den igen og glimtede tavst. Det lignede ikke en hval — og alligevel, var det Moby Dick? tænkte Daggoo. Igen gik fantomet ned, men da det dukkede op endnu en gang, hylede den sorte mand med et dolkeagtigt skrig, der skræmte hver mand op af hans døs: »Der! Der igen! Der springer hun! Lige forude! Den Hvide Hval, den Hvide Hval!«

Ved dette styrtede sømændene ud på rånokkerne, som bier styrter ud på grenene, når de sværmer. Ahab stod barhovedet på bovsprydet i den glohede sol, den ene hånd stukket langt bagud, parat til at give sine ordrer til rorgængeren, og vendte sit ivrige blik derhen, hvor Daggoos udstrakte, ubevægelige arm pegede oppe fra højden.

Måske havde følget af den ene stille, ensomme stråle langsomt virket på Ahab, så han nu var parat til at forbinde tanker om mildhed og ro med det første syn af den bestemte hval, han jagtede; eller måske løb hans iver af med ham. Hvad end det var, gav han i det øjeblik, han tydeligt kunne se den hvide masse, med hurtig intensitet ordre til at sætte bådene i vandet.

De fire både var snart i vandet, Ahabs foran, alle roede hårdt mod deres bytte. Snart gik tingen ned, og mens vi ventede med løftede årer på, at den skulle dukke op igen — se! — steg den langsomt op igen på præcis det sted, hvor den var sunket. Næsten uden at tænke på Moby Dick i øjeblikket stirrede vi nu på det mest forbløffende fænomen, som de hemmelige have endnu har vist menneskeheden. En enorm geléagtig masse, flere furlongs lang og bred, af en glinsende flødefarve, lå og flød på vandet, med utallige lange arme, der strålede ud fra midten og krøllede og snoede sig som en rede af anacondaer, som om de famlede blindt efter enhver uheldig genstand inden for rækkevidde. Den havde intet ansigt eller forside, man kunne få øje på, ikke noget tænkeligt tegn på hverken følelse eller instinkt; den bølgede bare der på bølgerne, et overjordisk, formløst, tilfældigt genfærd af liv.

Mens den med en lav sugende lyd langsomt forsvandt igen, udbrød Starbuck, der stadig stirrede på det oprørte vand, hvor den var sunket, med vild stemme — »Jeg ville næsten hellere have set Moby Dick og kæmpet mod ham end have set dig, hvide genfærd!«
»Hvad var det, sir?« sagde Flask.
»Den store levende blæksprutte, som, siger man, kun få hvalfangerskibe nogensinde har set og er vendt tilbage til deres havne for at fortælle om.«
Men Ahab sagde intet. Han vendte sin båd og sejlede tilbage til skibet. De andre fulgte tavst efter.

Hvilken overtro kaskelotfangere i almindelighed end har knyttet til synet af denne ting, er én ting sikker: Fordi et glimt af den er så overordentlig sjældent, har netop det faktum i sig selv gjort meget for at give den et præg af ondt varsel. Den ses så sjældent, at selv om hver eneste af dem erklærer den for det største levende væsen i havet, har meget få mere end de allerdiffuseste forestillinger om dens virkelige natur og form. Alligevel tror de, at den giver kaskelotten dens eneste føde. Andre slags hvaler finder deres føde over vandet, hvor mennesker kan se dem æde; men spermacethvalen får al sin føde i ukendte zoner under overfladen, og hvad den nøjagtigt består af, kan kun udledes af slutninger. Somme tider, når han er hårdt trængt, vil han kaste op, hvad man mener er blæksprutteens løsrevne arme, nogle af dem over tyve, endda tredive, fod lange. Hvalfangerne forestiller sig, at uhyret, som disse arme tilhørte, som regel hænger fast ved havbunden med dem, og at kaskelotten, i modsætning til andre arter, har tænder, for at den kan angribe det og rive det fra hinanden.

Der synes at være nogen grund til at forestille sig, at den store Kraken hos biskop Pontoppodan til sidst kan vise sig at være en blæksprutte. Måden, biskoppen beskriver den på — som skiftevis stigende og synkende, med visse andre enkeltheder, han giver — i alt dette svarer de to til hinanden. Men der må tages meget højde for den utrolige størrelse, han tillægger den.

Visse naturforskere, som kun vagt har hørt rygter om det mystiske væsen, der tales om her, regner det blandt blæksprutterne, som det i visse ydre henseender rigtignok ser ud til at høre til — men kun som stammens Anak, dens bibelske kæmpe.
